title: New Mexico Deploys JTIP Workforce Grants to Support Quantum Hardware Hiring at IonQ and Bandelier Technologies - Quantum Computing Report
gist: Economic Development New Mexico approved more than $12 million in Q1 FY2027 Job Training Incentive Program awards to 33 firms, including $160,951 for three IonQ engineering hires in Albuquerque (about $93/hour) and $151,078 across two awards for four Bandelier Technologies trainees in Santa Fe. JTIP reimburses 50-90% of wages for up to six months, part of New Mexico's push to commercialize Sandia and Los Alamos deep-tech IP alongside DARPA QBI matching funds.

insights.claim: Economic Development New Mexico approved more than $12 million in Job Training Incentive Program (JTIP) funding for Q1 FY2027 across 33 firms. Cabinet Secretary Rob Black said more than half of them are in priority innovation fields: quantum information science, fusion energy and aerospace defense.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: New Mexico is steering incentive money toward quantum, fusion and defense, which supports cluster formation around its national labs.
insights.locator: The workforce subsidies integrate with the state’s broader capital incentives

insights.claim: JTIP reimburses expanding employers for 50% to 90% of eligible employee wages for up to six months of structured technical onboarding.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Wage subsidies lower the cost of hiring for quantum firms setting up New Mexico operations.
insights.locator: The JTIP initiative reimburses expanding employers

insights.claim: IonQ received $160,951 under JTIP to subsidize three hardware-engineering and system-operations roles in Albuquerque at an average of $93/hour (about $193,000 a year). IonQ is an inaugural resident partner at the new 35,000-square-foot Roadrunner Quantum Lab in Albuquerque's downtown Innovation District.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: IonQ (IONQ) is expanding its physical footprint in New Mexico, though this headcount (three trainees) is small.

insights.claim: Bandelier Technologies, a Santa Fe spinout from Los Alamos National Laboratory via the New Mexico LEEP program, builds photonic quantum radar, quantum sensing instruments and AI-integrated metasurface antennas for GPS-denied navigation and defense monitoring. It received $117,616 in August for three trainees ($68/hour) and $33,462 in September for another specialist ($59/hour).
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: This is an early-stage defense quantum sensing player to watch, as GPS-denied navigation is a growing defense procurement theme.

insights.claim: The JTIP awards follow earlier EDNM technology commercialization grants, including $1.2 million across regional quantum startups. Together they reflect New Mexico's sustained policy to commercialize deep-tech IP from Sandia National Laboratories and Los Alamos National Laboratory.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: National-lab IP commercialization is New Mexico's competitive angle in the state race for quantum clusters.
insights.locator: The workforce awards follow earlier state technology commercialization grants

insights.claim: New Mexico's workforce subsidies sit alongside broader capital incentives, including standing matching-fund programs for performers in DARPA's Quantum Benchmarking Initiative (QBI).
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: State matching funds for QBI performers can sway where QBI-backed quantum companies site their operations.
insights.locator: The workforce subsidies integrate with the state’s broader capital incentives
